articles.title: What happens after my solar installation fails an inspection?
articles.summary: Explains the steps Brightline takes after a failed inspection, including correction timelines, re-inspection scheduling, and any associated fees.
articles.question: My installation just failed its municipal inspection. What does this mean for my project, and what will Brightline do next?
articles.answer:
Understanding a Failed Inspection

A failed inspection means the local Authority Having Jurisdiction (AHJ) found one or more items on your installation that do not meet the applicable electrical, building, or fire code at the time of inspection. This is more common than many customers expect—roughly 12% of Brightline installations require at least one re-inspection—and it does not automatically indicate a serious problem with your system.

What Brightline Does Immediately

Within one business day of receiving the failed inspection report, your Brightline Project Coordinator will:

  • Review the inspector's correction notice (also called a "red tag" or "NOV").
  • Classify each deficiency as minor (paperwork or labeling), moderate (wiring adjustment), or major (structural or equipment change).
  • Contact you via email and the Brightline Home app with a summary and an estimated correction timeline.

Correction and Re-Inspection Timelines

Deficiency ClassTypical Correction WindowRe-Inspection Scheduled Within
Minor1–3 business days5 business days
Moderate3–7 business days10 business days
Major7–21 business days21 business days

Fees

Brightline covers the cost of the first re-inspection at no charge to you. If a second re-inspection is required due to the same uncorrected item, a $150 administrative fee may apply. Your coordinator will notify you before any fee is assessed.

Impact on Interconnection

Your utility interconnection application is paused while a failed inspection is open. Once the AHJ issues a passing inspection certificate, Brightline resubmits the documentation automatically. For context on interconnection timelines, see Utility Interconnection Delays – Summer 2025.

articles.title: Why do solar inspections fail, and can I do anything to prevent it?
articles.summary: Lists the most common reasons Brightline installations receive a failed inspection notice and explains what customers can do before and during the inspection to help it go smoothly.
articles.question: I heard that solar inspections can fail for all sorts of reasons. What are the most common causes, and is there anything I can do to help make sure my inspection passes?
articles.answer:
Most Common Reasons for a Failed Inspection

Based on Brightline's internal records from 2023–2024, the following issues account for over 80% of all failed inspection notices:

  1. Missing or incorrect labeling – Rapid-shutdown labels, conduit markers, or AC/DC disconnect labels that do not match the approved permit drawings.
  2. Conductor sizing discrepancy – Wire gauge installed in the field differs from what is specified on the stamped electrical plan.
  3. Improper rapid-shutdown device placement – The RSC (Rapid Shutdown Controller) is located more than the code-allowed distance from the service entrance.
  4. Roof penetration sealing – Lag bolts or conduit entry points not sealed with approved weatherproofing material.
  5. Permit document mismatch – The on-site permit package does not include the most recently approved revision of the drawings. This has become more common since AHJs began requiring digital uploads; see New Interconnection Document Upload Requirement for details.
  6. Ground-fault or arc-fault protection gaps – A GFCI or AFCI breaker required by the 2023 NEC amendment is absent or incorrectly sized.

What You Can Do Before the Inspection

  • Ensure the inspector has clear, unobstructed access to the roof, attic hatch, main electrical panel, and any sub-panels.
  • Confirm with your Brightline coordinator that the correct permit revision is posted at the job site or available digitally—your coordinator will send you a confirmation email the day before the scheduled inspection.
  • Keep pets secured and designated an adult (18+) to be present; inspectors will not proceed without an authorized occupant on-site.

Historic District Considerations

If your property is in a historic district, additional design criteria may apply that increase the chance of an AHJ correction notice. Review Request Historic District Permit Approval to understand those requirements before your inspection date.

articles.title: How do I reschedule my inspection after a failed inspection?
articles.summary: Explains the steps to book a re-inspection appointment after a failed municipal inspection and what to expect from Brightline during that process.
articles.question: My inspection failed and the inspector left a correction notice. How do I reschedule, and will Brightline handle the fixes before the re-inspection?
articles.answer:
What happens immediately after a failed inspection

Within 1 business day of receiving a failed inspection report from your local Authority Having Jurisdiction (AHJ), your Brightline Project Coordinator will email you a Correction Summary listing every cited deficiency, the permit code reference, and the corrective action Brightline will take. You do not need to contact your municipality directly.

How to reschedule through Brightline Home

  1. Open Brightline Home and tap My Project → Permits & Inspections.
  2. Locate the failed inspection entry (status shown as Correction Required) and tap Request Re-Inspection.
  3. Select your preferred date window. Re-inspection slots open 5–10 business days after the correction work is completed.
  4. Confirm the request. You will receive an email and in-app notification with the confirmed date within 2 business days.

Re-inspection fees

If the failure was due to a Brightline installation error, the re-inspection fee is covered at no charge to you. If the failure resulted from a change you requested after permit issuance, a $95 re-inspection coordination fee applies. This fee appears as a separate line item on your next invoice.

Timeframes

StepTypical Duration
Correction work completed3–7 business days
Re-inspection scheduled5–10 business days after corrections
Permit closed (pass)1–3 business days after re-inspection

For more detail on what happens once a re-inspection passes, see What happens after a failed inspection.

articles.title: Will a failed inspection delay when my solar system turns on?
articles.summary: Explains how a failed municipal inspection affects your system activation date and what Brightline does to minimize delays.
articles.question: My inspection didn't pass. Does this mean my solar panels won't be turned on yet, and how long could the delay be?
articles.answer:
Why activation is paused after a failed inspection

Brightline is required by law to obtain a final inspection approval and a Permission to Operate (PTO) letter from your utility before energizing your system. A failed inspection resets this clock, so your system will remain in Safe-Off mode until the re-inspection passes and PTO is granted.

Typical delay scenarios

  • Minor correction (e.g., labeling, wire management): 7–14 business days total before re-inspection.
  • Moderate correction (e.g., grounding conductor re-route, conduit adjustment): 14–21 business days.
  • Major correction (e.g., structural attachment revision requiring updated engineered drawings): 30–45 business days. A Brightline engineering review fee of $150 may apply if a new structural letter is needed.

How to track your status

You can monitor every milestone in real time inside Brightline Home under My Project → Permits & Inspections. Each stage displays an estimated completion date that updates automatically when Brightline submits documents to your AHJ.

Alerts and notifications during the delay

Because your system is not yet producing energy, any production alerts are automatically suppressed during this period to avoid confusion. Alerts will resume the first full day after activation. For background on how alerts work, see How do alert notifications work in Brightline Home.

Common reasons inspections fail

For a full breakdown of the most frequent inspection failures and how Brightline addresses them, see Why did my inspection fail — common reasons.

articles.title: How does the permit process work if my home is in a historic district?
articles.summary: Homes in historic districts require additional review steps before a solar permit can be issued, which extends the typical installation timeline.
articles.question: My home is in a historic district. How does the permit process work, and how long will it take?
articles.answer:
Historic District Permit Overview

Installing solar on a home in a designated historic district involves an extra layer of review beyond a standard municipal building permit. Brightline Solar manages this process on your behalf, but the additional steps do affect your timeline.

Steps in the Process

  1. Historic Review Board (HRB) Application: Before submitting your building permit, Brightline files a Certificate of Appropriateness (COA) application with your local Historic Review Board. This documents panel placement, color, and visibility from public rights-of-way.
  2. HRB Hearing: Most boards meet monthly. Your application is placed on the next available agenda, which can add 4–8 weeks to your timeline depending on meeting schedules.
  3. COA Approval: Once the HRB approves the design, Brightline submits the standard building permit with the COA attached.
  4. Standard Permit Issuance: Municipal review then proceeds normally (typically 2–4 weeks).

Typical Total Timeline

PhaseEstimated Duration
HRB Application Preparation1–2 weeks
HRB Review & Hearing4–8 weeks
Building Permit Issuance2–4 weeks
Total (estimated)7–14 weeks

What You Can Do

  • Check your project status anytime in Brightline Home → My Project → Permit Status.
  • Contact your Project Coordinator at permits@brightlinesolar.com if your HRB hearing date has not been confirmed within 10 business days of signing your contract.

For related permit timeline information, see Ground-Mount Permit Timeline Extension – Rural Zones.

articles.title: Are there extra design restrictions or fees for solar in a historic district?
articles.summary: Historic districts often impose specific design requirements and may carry additional permit fees that Brightline will outline in your project proposal.
articles.question: I heard that historic districts have special rules about what solar equipment looks like. Are there extra restrictions, and will I pay more in permit fees?
articles.answer:
Design Restrictions in Historic Districts

Historic Review Boards (HRBs) evaluate solar installations to ensure they do not adversely affect the historic character of a property or neighborhood. Common restrictions include:

  • Panel visibility: Panels must often be placed on rear or side roof slopes not visible from a public street or alley. Front-facing installations are frequently denied.
  • Panel color and finish: All-black panels with a low-glare anti-reflective coating (e.g., matte finish rated ≤ 5% reflectivity) are typically required. Standard blue-cell panels may be rejected.
  • Racking profile: Flush-mount, low-profile racking (maximum 4 inches above roof surface) is almost always required; tilt-up or elevated racking is rarely approved.
  • No visible conduit: All conduit runs must be concealed within the attic or interior of the structure wherever possible.

Additional Permit Fees

Historic district reviews carry fees separate from your standard building permit. Typical charges passed through to customers are:

  • COA Application Fee: $150–$400, billed by the municipality and reflected as a line item on your Brightline invoice under Permit & Inspection Fees.
  • Expedited HRB Review (optional): Some jurisdictions offer a $250 expedite fee to place your application on a special agenda, reducing wait time to approximately 2 weeks.

These fees are itemized in your project proposal and again on your final invoice. To understand how permit fees appear on your bill, see Understand Invoice Line Items and Ground-Mount Permit Fee Increase 2025.

Questions?

Contact your assigned Project Coordinator or email permits@brightlinesolar.com with your project ID for design guidance specific to your HRB jurisdiction.

articles.title: How long does it take to get solar approved in a historic district?
articles.summary: Historic district solar approvals involve an extra review layer and typically add 6–14 weeks to the standard permit timeline.
articles.question: I live in a historic district. How much longer will the permit process take compared to a regular installation?
articles.answer:
Why Historic Districts Take Longer

In addition to your local building permit, any home in a designated historic district requires review and approval from the relevant Historic Preservation Commission (HPC) or equivalent authority. Brightline cannot submit the standard permit until HPC approval is in hand, so the two processes run sequentially, not in parallel.

Typical Timeline Breakdown

StageEstimated Duration
Brightline design review & HPC application prep1–2 weeks
HPC public notice period3–4 weeks (required by most jurisdictions)
HPC hearing and written decision2–6 weeks
Standard building permit (after HPC approval)2–4 weeks

What Brightline Does During This Time

  • Your assigned Permit Coordinator will file the HPC application within 5 business days of your signed agreement.
  • You will receive status updates in the Brightline Home app under My Project > Permits > Historic Review Status.
  • If the HPC requests design modifications, Brightline's design team will respond within 10 business days.

What Can Cause Further Delays

Some commissions meet only monthly. If your application misses a submission cutoff, the HPC hearing may be pushed to the following meeting cycle. Your Permit Coordinator will flag this risk as soon as submission deadlines are confirmed.

For information on design changes that may be required, see Historic District Solar Design Restrictions and Fees. For guidance on what happens if an inspection fails after approval, see What Happens After a Failed Inspection.

articles.title: What are my options if the Historic Preservation Commission denies my solar application?
articles.summary: An HPC denial is not necessarily final — Brightline can help you appeal or redesign your system to meet preservation guidelines.
articles.question: The Historic Preservation Commission denied my solar permit application. Does this mean I can't get solar at all?
articles.answer:
A Denial Is Not Always the End

An initial Historic Preservation Commission (HPC) denial is disappointing, but it rarely means solar is impossible. Commissions typically deny applications because of visibility, panel placement, or equipment appearance — issues that can often be resolved through redesign or appeal.

Your Options After a Denial

  1. Formal Appeal: Most jurisdictions allow one administrative appeal, usually within 30 calendar days of the written denial. Brightline's permit team will review the denial letter and advise whether an appeal is viable at no additional charge.
  2. Redesign Submission: If the HPC identified specific objections, Brightline can revise panel placement, switch to low-profile all-black modules, or explore rear-roof and accessory-structure locations that may satisfy preservation standards. A redesign resubmission incurs a $175 HPC resubmission fee.
  3. Ground-Mount Alternative: If the home's roof is entirely restricted, a ground-mount system on a non-visible portion of your property may be approvable under separate guidelines. Note that ground-mount permitting carries its own timeline; see Ground-Mount Permit Timeline Extension in Rural Zones for context.

Next Steps

Within 3 business days of receiving your denial notice, your Brightline Permit Coordinator will contact you to schedule a review call. You can also view the denial reason and upload supporting documents in the Brightline Home app under My Project > Permits > HPC Decision.

For information on the full historic district permit process, see Historic District Solar Permit Process.

articles.title: What is the 'Monitoring Subscription' line on my invoice?
articles.summary: Explains what the Monitoring Subscription charge covers, how much it costs, and where to find more detail on your invoice.
articles.question: I noticed a line called 'Monitoring Subscription' on my latest Brightline invoice. What is this charge for, and is it mandatory?
articles.answer:
What the Monitoring Subscription Covers

The Monitoring Subscription line item is a recurring monthly fee that pays for continued access to the real-time production data, alerts, and remote diagnostics available in the Brightline Home app. Specifically, it funds:

  • Live and historical energy production graphs (updated every 5 minutes)
  • Automated alert notifications, including panel-level and microinverter offline alerts
  • Remote battery control and dispatch scheduling
  • Cloud storage of up to 10 years of performance data
  • Access to our 24/7 monitoring operations center, which proactively flags system anomalies

Current Pricing

As of January 2025, the standard Monitoring Subscription is $9.99 per month (plus applicable state taxes). Customers who purchased a Brightline Platinum system package prior to March 1, 2023 may see a grandfathered rate of $6.99 per month reflected on their invoice instead.

Is It Mandatory?

The subscription is required to maintain active monitoring and alert coverage. If you downgrade to a no-subscription status, real-time data and push notifications will be suspended within one billing cycle, though your system will continue to generate power normally.

Where to Find the Detail

In the Brightline Home app, go to Account → Billing → Invoice History, select any invoice, and tap View Line Item Detail to see the subscription period dates and any prorated adjustments. For a full guide to reading your invoice, see How to Read Your Brightline Invoice. If the amount looks different from a previous month, Why Is My Invoice Total Different from Last Month? may also help.

articles.title: Why did my Monitoring Subscription charge change or appear for the first time?

articles.question: My Monitoring Subscription charge is different from last month—or I never saw it before and it just appeared. Why is this happening?

Common Reasons the Charge Changed

Several events can cause the Monitoring Subscription line to change amount or appear for the first time:

Plan upgradeUpgrading from Basic to Premium Monitoring ($14.99/month) adds battery dispatch scheduling and priority support response.
Mid-cycle plan changeIf you changed plans partway through a billing period, you may see a prorated amount. See Prorated Charges: Mid-Cycle Plan Changes for details.
Rate adjustmentBrightline issued a rate update effective March 1, 2025; customers not on a grandfathered rate moved from $8.99 to $9.99/month.
Tax jurisdiction changeA change to your service address can alter the applicable state or local tax, shifting the total even if the base fee stayed the same.

What to Do If the Change Seems Wrong

  1. Open Brightline Home → Account → Billing → Invoice History and tap the affected invoice to review line-item dates and rates.
  2. Compare with your previous invoice using the Compare Invoices toggle at the top of the Invoice History screen.
  3. If you believe the charge is an error, you have 60 days from the invoice date to open a dispute via Account → Billing → Dispute an Invoice. For current dispute window rules, see Invoice Dispute Window Extension 2025.
  4. If you cannot resolve it in the app, contact Brightline Support at 1-800-555-0174 (Mon–Fri, 7 a.m.–8 p.m. ET) and reference invoice number and error code BL-INV-4031 if shown.

Canceling or Downgrading Your Subscription

To change your monitoring plan, go to Account → Monitoring Plan → Change Plan. Changes take effect at the start of the next billing cycle; you will not be charged a cancellation fee.

articles.title: Can I remove or downgrade my monitoring subscription?
articles.summary: Explains which monitoring subscription tiers can be changed or cancelled, how to request a change in the Brightline Home app, and what happens to your invoice after the change.
articles.question: I see a monitoring subscription line on my invoice every month. Can I remove it or switch to a cheaper plan? I don't think I'm using all the features it covers.
articles.answer:
Monitoring Subscription Tiers

Brightline offers three monitoring subscription tiers: Basic (included at no charge), Plus ($4.99/month), and Pro ($9.99/month). If your invoice shows a monitoring subscription charge, you are currently on Plus or Pro. Basic provides real-time production graphs and email alerts; Plus adds battery scheduling and SMS alerts; Pro adds advanced analytics, priority support response, and API data export.

How to Change or Remove Your Subscription

  1. Open Brightline Home and tap Account in the bottom navigation bar.
  2. Select Billing & Subscriptions, then tap Monitoring Plan.
  3. Choose a lower tier or select Basic (Free), then tap Confirm Change.

Changes take effect at the start of your next billing cycle. You will not receive a prorated refund for the remainder of the current cycle unless your account qualifies under our prorated charges policy — see Prorated Charges Policy Update 2025 for details.

Restrictions

  • If your system includes a Brightline Battery module, downgrading below Plus will disable remote battery scheduling controls in the app.
  • Monitoring subscriptions cannot be removed entirely if your loan agreement requires Pro-tier reporting — contact support to verify your loan terms.
  • Changes made within 24 hours of your billing date may not process until the following cycle.

If the charge appeared without you selecting an upgrade, please review Monitoring Subscription Charge Changed or Appeared Unexpectedly.

articles.title: Why am I still being charged for monitoring after closing my account or transferring my system?
articles.summary: Explains why a monitoring subscription line may continue to appear on invoices after an account closure or system ownership transfer, and the steps to resolve or dispute the charge.
articles.question: I closed my Brightline account (or transferred my solar system to a new homeowner) but I'm still seeing the monitoring subscription line on my invoice. Why is this charge still appearing and how do I get it stopped?
articles.answer:
Why the Charge May Continue

Monitoring subscriptions are billed one cycle in advance. If your account closure or system transfer was processed after your billing date, one final monitoring charge will appear on the next invoice. This is expected and does not indicate an error in most cases.

However, if you are seeing charges two or more cycles after your closure or transfer date, this may indicate one of the following:

  • The closure request is still pending — account closures can take up to 10 business days to fully process.
  • A linked loan agreement is keeping the account in an active-billing state.
  • The system transfer was submitted but not yet accepted by the new owner in their Brightline Home app.

How to Resolve the Charge

  1. Log in to Brightline Home and navigate to Account > Billing & Subscriptions to check your account status.
  2. If the status still shows Active, contact Brightline Support at 1-800-555-0198 with your account number and closure confirmation email.
  3. For system transfers, confirm the new owner has completed acceptance in their app; until they do, billing responsibility remains with the original account.

Disputing the Charge

If you believe the monitoring charge is an error, you can open a formal invoice dispute within 60 days of the charge date. See Invoice Dispute Window Extension 2025 for current dispute deadlines, and review What Happens to Monitoring and Alerts When I Close My Account for details on how monitoring services wind down after closure.

articles.title: Transfer Your Solar Agreement to a Home Buyer
articles.summary: Submit a transfer request in Brightline Home so that your financing agreement, monitoring access, and system ownership are reassigned to the buyer before closing.
articles.body:
Before you begin: You must be the primary account holder. The transfer request must be submitted at least 21 calendar days before your closing date. Both you and the buyer will need valid email addresses. If your account has an outstanding balance, it must be settled before the transfer can proceed — see Prorated Charges for Mid-Cycle Plan Changes for how charges are calculated up to your transfer date. A one-time Transfer Processing Fee of $195 applies and will appear on your final invoice.

  1. Open the Brightline Home app and tap Account in the bottom navigation bar.
  2. Select Financing & Agreements, then tap Initiate Home Sale Transfer.
  3. Enter your confirmed closing date and the buyer's full legal name and email address.
  4. Review the transfer summary, confirm the $195 Transfer Processing Fee, and tap Submit Request. You will receive a confirmation email with reference number TRF-XXXXXX within 15 minutes.
  5. Brightline will email the buyer a Buyer Acceptance Link within 2 business days. The buyer must complete identity verification and e-sign the assumption agreement.
  6. Once the buyer signs, Brightline reviews both parties' submissions. Allow up to 10 business days for final approval. You will receive a status update by email at each stage.
  7. On the approved transfer date, billing, monitoring alerts, and battery control access shift to the buyer's new account. Your account will be marked Transferred and all automatic payments will stop.

Troubleshooting

"Transfer Ineligible" error (code TRF-403): This usually means an unpaid invoice is blocking the request. Go to Account > Billing > Outstanding Invoices and clear any balance, then retry.

Buyer never received the Acceptance Link: Ask the buyer to check their spam folder. If the email is not found after 24 hours, contact Brightline Support and provide your TRF-XXXXXX reference number — an agent can resend the link or update the buyer's email address.

Closing date changed after submission: You can update the closing date up to 7 days before the original date via Account > Financing & Agreements > Manage Transfer. Changes within 7 days require a support call.

Monitoring alerts during the transfer window: Your alerts remain active until the transfer is finalized. The buyer will inherit your current alert settings; they can modify them after their account is activated. See How Alert Notifications Work in Brightline Home for details.

articles.title: Resolve a Rejected or Stalled Solar Transfer Before Closing
articles.summary: Follow these steps to diagnose and fix common reasons a home-sale transfer request is rejected or stops progressing, so you can meet your closing deadline.
articles.body:
Before you begin: Locate your Transfer Reference Number (TRF-XXXXXX) from the confirmation email sent when you first submitted the transfer. You will need this for all support interactions. If you have not yet started a transfer, see Transfer Your Solar Agreement to a Home Buyer first.

  1. Open Brightline Home, go to Account > Financing & Agreements > Manage Transfer, and note the status shown next to your TRF-XXXXXX request. Common statuses: Pending Buyer Signature, Under Review, Action Required, or Rejected.
  2. If status is Action Required, tap the yellow banner to view the specific item blocking progress. Common blockers include: unsigned loan assumption documents, a failed buyer identity check, or a missing government-issued ID upload from the buyer.
  3. If status is Rejected, tap View Rejection Reason. Rejections carry a reason code:
    • REJ-101 — Outstanding balance on seller account. Pay all invoices under Account > Billing, then tap Request Re-Review.
    • REJ-102 — Buyer credit check did not meet loan assumption threshold. The buyer must contact their lender or explore a cash payoff option; call Brightline Financing at 1-800-555-0174.
    • REJ-103 — Closing date is fewer than 5 business days away. Call Brightline Support immediately for an expedited review (additional $75 rush fee applies).
    • REJ-104 — System has an open service ticket (e.g., a failed inspection). The ticket must be resolved before transfer. See What Happens After a Failed Inspection.
  4. After resolving the blocker, return to Manage Transfer and tap Resubmit for Review. Allow up to 5 business days for re-evaluation.
  5. If the transfer is approved late and overlaps your closing date, notify your escrow agent that Brightline will issue a prorated final statement within 3 business days post-closing. The buyer's account activates automatically on the approved transfer date.
  6. Once complete, confirm that your access to the system in Brightline Home shows View Only — Transferred, and that you have received a Transfer Completion email. Retain this email for your real estate records.

Troubleshooting

Re-review stuck in "Under Review" for more than 5 business days: Contact Brightline Support by phone (1-800-555-0174, Mon–Fri 8 a.m.–7 p.m. ET) or via in-app chat. Provide your TRF-XXXXXX number and ask for an escalation to the Financing Transfer Team.

Buyer cannot complete identity verification: The buyer's Acceptance Link expires after 7 days. If it has expired, log in to Manage Transfer and select Resend Buyer Invitation to generate a fresh link.

You sold the home but forgot to initiate a transfer: Call Brightline Financing immediately at 1-800-555-0174. A retroactive transfer can be processed within 30 days of closing, though a $250 late-transfer fee applies and both the seller and buyer must be reachable to sign documents.
